mcqs.question: What's the scoped, correct move for guaranteeing read-your-writes?
options: Make every read in the system strongly consistent so nobody ever sees stale data
Route only the writer's own subsequent reads to the primary or a replica confirmed caught up
Disable replicas entirely until the write has propagated everywhere
Ask the user to manually refresh until the write appears
mcqs.explanation: The fix should be scoped to the writer, not applied system-wide. Forcing global strong consistency, disabling replicas, or telling the user to refresh either over-solves the problem at a huge cost or doesn't solve it at all.

mcqs.question: In the version-tagged routing approach, what determines which replica a read is sent to?
options: Whichever replica has the lowest current CPU usage
Always the primary, regardless of replica state
Whichever replica has applied a version at least as new as the write being read back
A replica chosen at random from the healthy pool
mcqs.explanation: The read path checks each replica's applied version against the write's version, and routes to the first one that's caught up — falling back to the primary only if none has. CPU usage, always-primary, and random selection all ignore the actual freshness guarantee the technique is built to provide.

mcqs.question: What's the downside of session-pinning compared to version-tagged routing?
options: It keeps sending that user's reads to the more-loaded primary for the whole window, even for reads unrelated to the write
It requires every replica to expose a comparable version number
It cannot be implemented without changing the write path
It only works for a single specific database vendor
mcqs.explanation: Session-pinning is simple precisely because it doesn't check replica state — but that means it pins every read during the window to the primary, not just reads of the written data. Version-tagged routing is the one that needs comparable replica positions; pinning needs no write-path changes and isn't vendor-specific.

mcqs.question: What's wrong with solving read-your-writes by making every read strongly consistent?
options: It pays a global latency and scalability cost to fix a problem scoped to one user's own reads
It is technically infeasible in any real database
It only works for read-heavy workloads, never write-heavy ones
It has no downside and is always the right call
mcqs.explanation: Read-your-writes only needs to hold for the writer's own subsequent reads — forcing every read through a strongly consistent path pays that cost for all users, all the time, to fix a narrow case. It's feasible, not workload-restricted, and comes with a real scalability cost.
